ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Participants were recruited as part of the Africa Long Life Study (ALLS), a longitudinal study of young adults from throughout Kenya, Namibia, and South Africa, including rural villages, informal settlements, cities, and suburbs 33 .

> Participants could receive the survey via an SMS or email link sent to their devices; however, most participants were reached by local research assistants who administered the survey on electronic tablets or paper.

> Participants had a mean age of 21.25 (SD = 1.10) and approximately half identified as female.

> Participants were asked "In general, would you say your health is…" and provided the following response options on a five-point scale: Poor, Fair, Good, Very Good, Excellent.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Human well-being depends on the natural environment, yet evidence on how nature supports human life comes almost entirely from Western, industrialized societies-not from the regions facing the greatest ecological impacts of climatic change.

We assessed the importance of nature for ten life domains spanning four dimensions (Cultural, Community, Instrumental, Personal) among a sample of emerging adults in Kenya, Namibia, and South Africa (N = 2,792).
Most participants rated nature as important for at least one domain, while about one-third rated nature as important for all ten.

Greater importance of nature in the Cultural dimension was associated with greater life satisfaction, while greater importance in Cultural, Community, and Instrumental dimensions was associated with greater climate anxiety, over and above subjective connectedness to nature, religiosity, and socioeconomic status.

Findings suggest nature plays an important role in the lives of emerging adults in Sub-Saharan Africa, which may support wellbeing while making the risks associated with climate change more distressing.
Human flourishing and well-being depend on the natural environment.
At the most fundamental level, nature sustains life by maintaining clean air, water, and soil, regulating ecological processes, and reducing the impacts of natural hazards.

Beyond these essential functions, nature supports the material and psychological foundations of everyday life by providing food, livelihoods, and places for recreation, while also shaping identity, health, family and community life, and spiritual, cultural, and religious practices [1] [2] [3] .
text.formatted: Beyond these essential functions, nature supports the material and psychological foundations of everyday life by providing food, livelihoods, and places for recreation, while also shaping identity, health, family and community life, and spiritual, cultural, and religious practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> .

text.text: Both the natural environment and people's relationships with nature are increasingly threatened by ecological and climatic change, posing particular risks to communities that depend on nature across various domains of life 4, 5 .
text.formatted: Both the natural environment and people's relationships with nature are increasingly threatened by ecological and climatic change, posing particular risks to communities that depend on nature across various domains of life <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: Yet, despite these growing threats, little is known about how nature supports material and psychological functioning across these diverse domains of life in the Majority World, the regions most affected by ecological and climatic change, including Africa, Asia, the Middle East, and Latin America.
Connections with nature represent both a vital source of well-being and a source of vulnerability to the psychological impacts of ecological threats and climate change.

On the one hand, studies reveal robust associations between indicators of well-being (e.g., life satisfaction, self-reported health) with time spent in nature 6, 7 and with subjective connectedness to nature 8- 10 .
text.formatted: On the one hand, studies reveal robust associations between indicators of well-being (e.g., life satisfaction, self-reported health) with time spent in nature <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> and with subjective connectedness to nature <ref type="bibr">8- 10</ref> .

text.text: On the other hand, the psychological impacts of ecological risks and climate change more strongly affect individuals who feel a greater connection with nature 11, 12 , and pose increased risks for the health and well-being of communities dependent on nature in essential domains of life 13 .
text.formatted: On the other hand, the psychological impacts of ecological risks and climate change more strongly affect individuals who feel a greater connection with nature <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> , and pose increased risks for the health and well-being of communities dependent on nature in essential domains of life <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: These studies provide valuable insights but are limited to a near-exclusive sampling of participants from Western, industrialized contexts, a trend reflected in the broader environmental psychological literature 14 .
text.formatted: These studies provide valuable insights but are limited to a near-exclusive sampling of participants from Western, industrialized contexts, a trend reflected in the broader environmental psychological literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: To illustrate, a review of 174 studies of nature's effects on well-being included only a single study conducted with participants from the African continent and only two studies were conducted in low-middle-income countries 15 .
text.formatted: To illustrate, a review of 174 studies of nature's effects on well-being included only a single study conducted with participants from the African continent and only two studies were conducted in low-middle-income countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: This is notable because individuals in Western societies engage in lifestyles that depend on fewer direct connections with the natural environment 16 and also live in the regions least likely to experience the impacts of climate change 17, 18 .
text.formatted: This is notable because individuals in Western societies engage in lifestyles that depend on fewer direct connections with the natural environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> and also live in the regions least likely to experience the impacts of climate change <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> .

text.text: Dominant conceptualizations of human-nature relationships have focused on greenspace or subjective connectedness to nature 15, 19 , with far less attention to the diverse ways nature supports material and psychological function across domains of life in Majority World contexts.
text.formatted: Dominant conceptualizations of human-nature relationships have focused on greenspace or subjective connectedness to nature <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> , with far less attention to the diverse ways nature supports material and psychological function across domains of life in Majority World contexts.

text.text: Across African societies, for example, nature's importance in life extends beyond exposure to greenspace or feelings of connectedness to nature.

African indigenous religions and relational philosophies describe people as embedded within communities that encompass land, plants and animals, ancestors, and spiritual beings, linking personal and collective well-being with responsibilities of care toward the natural environment [20] [21] [22] .
text.formatted: African indigenous religions and relational philosophies describe people as embedded within communities that encompass land, plants and animals, ancestors, and spiritual beings, linking personal and collective well-being with responsibilities of care toward the natural environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> .

text.text: These ideas are reflected in empirical accounts from contemporary African populations: emerging adults in Namibia and Kenya report that one's relationship with nature is an important aspect of Ubuntu, a cultural value emphasizing communalism 23 , while smallholder farmers in Tanzania report that nature supports a number of domains of life, including spiritual experiences, cultural identity, social cohesion, sense of place, emotional well-being, recreation, food, and economic opportunities 24.
text.formatted: These ideas are reflected in empirical accounts from contemporary African populations: emerging adults in Namibia and Kenya report that one's relationship with nature is an important aspect of Ubuntu, a cultural value emphasizing communalism <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> , while smallholder farmers in Tanzania report that nature supports a number of domains of life, including spiritual experiences, cultural identity, social cohesion, sense of place, emotional well-being, recreation, food, and economic opportunities <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref>.

text.text: These perspectives and the available empirical evidence suggest that the ways people depend on, connect to, and value nature are multidimensional, culturally embedded, and consequential for how ecological change is experienced.

Sustainability science and policy that reduce human-nature relationships to economic value, greenspace, and subjective connectedness risk overlooking the many other ways that nature supports human well-being, and the many ways that communities in the Majority World are vulnerable to ecological and climatic change.

The present study surveys 2,792 emerging adults in Kenya, Namibia and South Africa to examine the importance of nature across 10 domains of life that span cultural, community, instrumental, and personal dimensions.

We examine the dimensional structure of importance ratings, and their associations with life satisfaction, self-reported health, and climate anxiety, over and above subjective connectedness to nature, religiosity, and socioeconomic status.
The data map humannature connections and their health and well-being correlates in difficult-to-reach samples of emerging adults in Sub-Saharan Africa.

text.text: Participants rated nature as being overwhelmingly important across a wide variety of life domains, including spiritual, cultural, and religious beliefs and practices, family and community activities, self-identity, mental and physical health, enjoyment and recreation, food security, and financial gain (Figure 1, Panel A).

text.text: In the total sample, 96.5% of participants rated nature to be important or very important for at least one domain, and approximately one-third rated nature to be important or very important for all ten (31.4%).
The proportion of participants for whom nature was important for all ten domains was somewhat higher in the Kenyan sample (39.4%) compared to the Namibian (22.9%) and South African samples (31.0%).

While mean importance ratings only spanned a range of 0.51 scale points (out of 5), the domains of mental and physical health and food security were reliably rated as most important in all three samples.

text.text: There were, however, qualitative differences in which associations were statistically significant in each country.
We summarize these exploratory differences briefly.
While life satisfaction was associated with nature's importance in the Cultural dimension in the total sample, this association was not found in South Africa.

While self-reported general health was not associated with any Nature in Life dimensions in the total sample, it was associated with the Community dimension in Namibia and the Instrumental domain in South Africa.

While ratings of climate change affecting one's daily life were associated with the Cultural and Community dimensions in the total sample, only the Cultural dimension was significant in all three countries, while in Kenya the Instrumental dimension was also significant, and in Namibia, the Community dimension was also significant.

While negative emotions about climate change was associated with the Cultural and Community dimensions in the total sample, this was only true in Kenya-none of the dimensions were associated with climate emotions in Namibia or South Africa.

Finally, while climate worry was associated with the Cultural, Community, and Instrumental dimensions in the full sample, different combinations of dimensions were significant in each of the three countries.
These results provide preliminary evidence that nature's link to well-being and climate anxiety may differ-albeit to a small degree-across three Sub-Saharan African countries.

Across 2,792 emerging adults in Kenya, Namibia, and South Africa, nature was rated to be important across ten domains of life, including spiritual, cultural, and religious beliefs and practices, family and community activities, self-identity, mental and physical health, recreation, and food security and financial gain.
These domains empirically clustered into four dimensions (Cultural, Community, Instrumental, and Personal), three of which were reliably associated with measures of well-being and climate anxiety.

Specifically, we found that higher ratings of the importance of nature in the Cultural dimension were associated with greater life satisfaction, while greater importance in the Cultural, Community, and Instrumental dimensions were associated with measures of climate anxiety-over and above sociodemographic variables, global subjective connectedness to nature, religiosity, and socioeconomic status.
Overall findings were broadly similar across countries, although modest country-level variation was evident for several outcomes.

This portrait of human-environment connections in Sub-Saharan Africa suggests that nature is embedded in multiple domains of life that support human flourishing, and climate anxiety may reflect an awareness of risk to the ecological foundations of individual and collective well-being in these populations.
These data make a descriptive contribution to basic knowledge about human connection with nature.
For emerging adults in Sub-Saharan Africa, nature is important for functioning across nearly every domain of life.
For 96.5% of participants, nature was important for at least one domain of life, and for roughly one-third of participants, nature was important for all ten domains.
This conceptual breadth is not captured in current operationalizations of connections to nature as exposure to greenspace or as a global sense of subjective connectedness 15, 19.
text.formatted: This conceptual breadth is not captured in current operationalizations of connections to nature as exposure to greenspace or as a global sense of subjective connectedness <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref>.

text.text: Correlations between the Nature in Life dimensions and the Inclusion of Nature in Self measure were weak, suggesting that perceived importance of nature in specific domains of life and global subjective connectedness to nature capture related but distinct aspects of human-nature relationships.

Approaches that do not consider the multidimensionality of connectedness to nature may overlook the qualitatively different ways in which nature supports human flourishing, and thus the qualitatively different risks presented by ecological and climatic change.

The Nature in Life framework developed here supports recent advances that expand these perspectives to include the functional, cultural, relational, and material ways in which people depend on nature and may therefore be affected by environmental change 22, [29] [30] [31].
text.formatted: The Nature in Life framework developed here supports recent advances that expand these perspectives to include the functional, cultural, relational, and material ways in which people depend on nature and may therefore be affected by environmental change <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Of the four Nature in Life dimensions, those pertaining to community and cultural activities were more reliably associated with well-being and climate anxiety than were those pertaining to instrumental and personal activities.
This was true of seven of eight significant effects in the main "baseline" models.

This pattern suggests a distinction between dimensions that reflect nature's role in relational, cultural, and socially embedded aspects of life and those that reflect more personal or material functions.

Community and Cultural dimensions showed more consistent associations with well-being and climate anxiety than Personal and Instrumental dimensions, suggesting that nature may exert particularly strong influences when it supports shared meanings, social relationships, and culturally significant practices.

One might expect the collective pathway to be strongest in populations for which collective activities in nature have no substitute-either because cultural knowledge is embodied in a traditional practice, such as caribou hunting among the Inuit 32 , or tied to specific natural sites.
text.formatted: One might expect the collective pathway to be strongest in populations for which collective activities in nature have no substitute-either because cultural knowledge is embodied in a traditional practice, such as caribou hunting among the Inuit <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> , or tied to specific natural sites.

text.text: Thus, the pathways through which nature affects well-being should differ across cultural contexts, further demonstrating the value of a multidimensional view of connectedness to nature.
Results across the three sample countries in the present study were generally consistent.
Participants in Kenya, Namibia, and South Africa, on average, rated nature as more important in Instrumental and Personal dimensions than Cultural and Community dimensions.
And the Nature in Life dimension by country interaction terms only explained up to 1.8% additional variance in well-being and climate anxiety.
Still, within this small range of variance, differences between the three countries were observed.

Kenyans showed the greatest number of significant independent associations between Nature in Life dimensions and well-being and climate anxiety (seven compared to five and four significant effects for Namibia and South Africa, respectively).
The Nature in Life dimensions associated with outcome variables were also found to modestly differ between countries.

For example, general self-reported health was not associated with any Nature in Life dimensions in Kenya but was associated with the Community dimension in Namibia and Instrumental dimension in South Africa.
Likewise, negative emotions about climate change were associated with the Cultural and Community dimensions in Kenya, but with no dimensions in Namibia and South Africa.

We take these exploratory results as suggestive that nature might affect well-being via different pathways across countries in Sub-Saharan Africa-a possibility with implications for future research, as well as advocacy and policymaking.
These findings contribute to ongoing policy discourse on nature's contributions to domains of life that are not represented in markets and thus pose difficulties for economic quantification 1, 22 .
text.formatted: These findings contribute to ongoing policy discourse on nature's contributions to domains of life that are not represented in markets and thus pose difficulties for economic quantification <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> .

text.text: Among emerging adults in Sub-Saharan Africa, it is precisely these difficultto-quantify connections with nature that may be most important for individual well-being.
Ecological risk assessments and climate adaptation initiatives are increasingly recognizing noneconomic contributions of nature to cultural heritage, identity, and ways of life 18 .
text.formatted: Ecological risk assessments and climate adaptation initiatives are increasingly recognizing noneconomic contributions of nature to cultural heritage, identity, and ways of life <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> .

text.text: These efforts can be assisted by greater scientific research documenting nature's contributions to the functioning and well-being of populations at risk of ecological and climate disruption.
Several limitations qualify these conclusions.
The data are cross-sectional, which limits conclusions about causality, although results were robust to analyses controlling for several potentially confounding variables.
Self-reported ratings of nature's importance were compressed near ceiling, restricting exploitable variance for analysis.

Future research may seek to increase item difficulty as one way to improve the psychometric properties of this measure (for example, asking the frequency with which nature is used in each domain of life and its centrality to the execution of activities in that domain).

Finally, the generalizability of these results to Western, industrialized populations and to other populations in Africa and the Majority World is not yet known-a fascinating frontier for future research to explore.

Beyond quantifying current connections with nature and their contributions to human flourishing and well-being, it will be informative to document how connections with nature evolve over the lifespan and within communities across time as they face continued economic and environmental change.

The Africa Long Life Study affords a rare capacity to collect such data, supported by investments into an infrastructure of collaborative research partnerships in communities across Sub-Saharan Africa.

The present study shows that nature is perceived as relevant to cultural, community, instrumental, and personal domains of life, and that these domains are not reducible to subjective connectedness to nature.

These results provide a foundation for a multidimensional and globally inclusive science of human-nature relationships that can support governance efforts to mitigate and adapt to environmental change.

text.text: Surveys were administered in English, a common language of education in all three countries.

Participants could receive the survey via an SMS or email link sent to their devices; however, most participants were reached by local research assistants who administered the survey on electronic tablets or paper.

This procedure allowed access to individuals and regions who would not otherwise be accessible through strictly online recruitment procedures, affording a more representative sample of young adults in the three countries.

Variables used in this study included participants' age, gender (female, male, other), country (Kenya, Namibia, South Africa), residential location (village, town, city), home language family (Afro-Asiatic, Bantu, Indo-European, Khoe-Kwadi, Nilotic), employment status (student, working, studying and working, not employed or studying), and recruitment source (research assistant, online).
Analyses proceeded in four stages.
First, we summarized item-level ratings of the importance of nature across the ten domains of life.

Second, we examined the dimensional structure of the importance of nature items using exploratory factor analysis, which revealed a multidimensional factor structure defined by Cultural, Community, Instrumental, and Personal dimensions.

Third, we examined the associations between the resulting four dimensions and measures of well-being and climate anxiety, in a series of models controlling for sociodemographic covariates and potential third variables.
Fourth, we examined the variability in these associations across the three sample countries.
The ten domains of life shared conceptual and empirical overlap, so we used exploratory factor analysis to explore the dimensional structure of the ten items.
Results are summarized here and a complete account is provided in the Supplemental Material.
A parallel analysis was conducted on the 2,792 (participants) x 10 (domains of life) Pearson correlation matrix using a maximum likelihood specification.

Parallel analysis compares eigenvalues from the observed correlation matrix with those derived from a random matrix of the same dimensions, retaining only factors that account for more variance than would be expected by chance 37 .
text.formatted: Parallel analysis compares eigenvalues from the observed correlation matrix with those derived from a random matrix of the same dimensions, retaining only factors that account for more variance than would be expected by chance <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> .

text.text: Parallel analysis suggested a four-factor solution consisting of a three-item "Cultural" factor (cultural, spiritual, religious), a one-item "Community" factor, a two-item "Instrumental" factor (food, economic), and a four-item "Personal" factor (health, recreation, identity, family).

The four-factor model cumulatively explained 64% of total variance, with the following measurement fit metrics: χ² (30) = 717.18, p < .001; CFIRobust = .94; RMSEARobust = 0.089; [0.082, 0.097]; SRMR = 0.040.
